strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem framing: FT-Dojo is the first benchmark to treat end-to-end LLM fine-tuning (joint data curation + training configuration + iterative refinement) as an agentic task, going beyond prior MLE-focused benchmarks (MLE-Bench, DSBench) that assume fixed datasets.

The benchmark is comprehensive and carefully engineered: 13 tasks across 5 diverse domains (math, patent, chemistry, finance, table QA), with a modular sandbox architecture (Meta API, Data Repository, Evaluator), clear task specifications, and extensive appendix documentation of data sources, decontamination procedures, and dataset statistics, supporting extensibility and reasonable reproducibility of the environment itself.

FT-Agent's three-stage design (structured iteration planning, fail-fast progressive validation, structured feedback analysis) is a sensible, well-motivated response to concrete failure modes identified in general-purpose agents (OpenHands), and the paper provides a fair, controlled comparison by equipping OpenHands with identical fine-tuning tools/primitives.

The empirical study is fairly extensive: main comparison against three baseline paradigms (base model, human-expert Manual SFT, tool-augmented OpenHands), ablations over data scale, backbone LLM, and model size (7B vs 3B), plus quantitative exploration-efficiency metrics (loops, improvement rate, cost).

The qualitative case studies (Sections 4.4, Appendix D) are a genuine strength — they go beyond aggregate metrics to trace decision trajectories (e.g., PI4PC "shotgun debugging" vs Mol_Edit cumulative learning), offering nuanced, honest insight into both agentic capabilities (cross-domain data transfer) and clear limitations (causal reasoning gaps, myopic planning causing data collapse), which strengthens the paper's scientific contribution beyond a simple leaderboard result.
weaknesses: No variance/repeated-trial reporting: all main results (Table 2), ablations, and case studies appear to be based on single runs, despite LLM agents and stochastic training being inherently noisy. Several performance gaps between FT-Agent and baselines are small (e.g., PI4PC tied at 44.00, Financial QA where Manual SFT wins by a few points), making it hard to assess whether the reported '10/13 tasks' superiority is statistically meaningful rather than noise.

Mixed/inconsistent results undercut the 'significantly outperforms' framing: Table 5 shows OpenHands outperforming FT-Agent on multiple Chemistry metrics (Mol_Edit Tanimoto, Reaction FTS/BLEU/Accuracy), which is acknowledged but somewhat softens the paper's central claim of consistent superiority.

Reproducibility concerns due to heavy reliance on closed, frontier proprietary models with non-standard/unclear version identifiers (GPT-5.2, GPT-5, GPT-4o-mini as both backbone and LLM-judge) whose behavior can silently change over time or become unavailable, undermining long-term reproducibility of the reported numbers; cost of replicating experiments with these models is also non-trivial and not fully quantified beyond per-task dollar estimates.

Very small test sets for some tasks (e.g., AIME 2025 test set has only 15 samples; several PANORAMA/ChemCoT/TableBench splits also have only 25–50 test samples), which severely limits the statistical power and reliability of accuracy differences, especially for the headline AIME result (13.3% on 15 samples corresponds to just ~2 correct answers).

The Manual SFT baseline is constrained to a restrictive 'two-pass' protocol that may not reflect realistic best-practice human expert workflows (which typically involve more iterative refinement), potentially biasing the comparison in FT-Agent's favor; this limitation is not clearly justified as representative of real-world deployment.

FT-Agent's design was explicitly derived from observed failure modes of OpenHands within FT-Dojo itself, raising a risk that the framework is somewhat overfit to the specific benchmark tasks rather than being a generally robust methodology, which is not addressed via held-out or out-of-distribution task evaluation.

Limited backbone/model diversity in ablations: robustness across model scale is only tested with one additional 3B model and one alternative backbone (GPT-4o), leaving open questions about generalization to other model families/architectures (e.g., open-source backbones, other LLM families).

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel and useful task formulation: treating end-to-end LLM fine-tuning (data curation + training configuration + iterative refinement) as an interactive agent environment, going beyond fixed-dataset MLE benchmarks like MLE-Bench/DSBench.
Reasonably broad task suite (13 tasks, 5 domains) with clear task specifications and pluggable evaluator interface, which could support future extensibility.

The three-stage FT-Agent design (strategy proposal, fail-fast validation, structured feedback analysis) is a sensible, well-motivated engineering response to observed failure modes of general-purpose coding agents.
Appendix provides substantial detail on data sources, decontamination procedures, baseline implementation, and full prompts, which aids reproducibility of the described pipeline.

The case studies (e.g., PI4PC 'shotgun debugging' trace, Mol_Edit cumulative learning trace) are a genuinely interesting and honest qualitative contribution, illustrating both capability and clear limitations (pattern-matching vs. causal reasoning) rather than only touting success.
weaknesses: No repeated trials or variance estimates are reported anywhere; given single runs and very small evaluation sets (e.g., AIME test = 15 samples, Mol_Edit test = 50, Vis test = 25), reported percentage-point differences (including the headline '0% -> 13.3%' AIME result, which is 2/15 correct) are not shown to be statistically meaningful, undermining the core empirical claims.

The comparison across methods is not clearly matched in exploration budget/fairness: Manual SFT is explicitly restricted to a 'two-pass' protocol while FT-Agent runs ~6-9 iterations, and OpenHands times out or is cut off after far fewer effective loops (Table 3, Table 6). This asymmetry inflates FT-Agent's apparent superiority over the human baseline in particular, since the disparity is partly a budget artifact rather than purely an architectural one.

No ablation isolates the individual contribution of each of the three proposed FT-Agent mechanisms (iteration planning, fail-fast validation, feedback analysis); it is therefore unclear which mechanism(s) actually drive the reported gains versus simply having more effective iterations from any one of them.

FT-Agent's own reported behavior undercuts the 'expert-like diagnosis' narrative: the PI4PC trace (Table 7) shows the agent cycling through interventions with hedged, non-causal language and eventually reverting to baseline configuration with 'no improvement,' which is presented as illustrative of limitations but also suggests that many 'wins' elsewhere in Table 2 may stem from lucky configuration choices rather than principled diagnosis.

Some metrics undercut the overall narrative without adequate discussion — e.g., FT-Agent underperforms OpenHands substantially on Reaction (FTS 18.11 vs 35.59, Acc 38 vs 60) and Mol_Opt Reaction, and the SR/other differences are not analyzed with the same rigor applied to 'win' cases, giving a somewhat cherry-picked framing of results.

Reliance on closed-source, versioned backbones (GPT-5.2, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-5-as-judge) for both the agent and the evaluation judge raises reproducibility concerns, since these models can change or become unavailable, and no inter-rater/judge reliability check is reported for the LLM-as-judge scoring used across diverse domains (chemistry, finance, patents).
The efficiency/cost comparison (Table 3) reports only 'iterative' cost, excluding GPU/compute cost, which likely dominates total resource use and could change the efficiency conclusions if included.

The only general-purpose baseline is OpenHands; broader comparison against other recent agentic ML/data-science frameworks would strengthen the claim that purpose-built design is necessary rather than simply better prompting/scaffolding of any agent.

The Impact Statement is generic and does not substantively engage with the specific dual-use risks introduced by an environment explicitly designed to lower the barrier to producing specialized fine-tuned models (e.g., for disallowed domains), beyond a brief acknowledgment.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely novel and underexplored problem: end-to-end autonomous LLM fine-tuning (data curation + training configuration + iterative refinement), distinct from prior MLE-agent benchmarks that assume fixed datasets.

FT-Dojo is a well-engineered environment with a clear formalization (Meta API, Data Repository, Evaluator), sandboxed reproducible execution, and an extensible task/metric interface spanning 5 diverse domains and 13 tasks.

FT-Agent's three mechanisms (structured iteration planning, fail-fast validation, structured feedback analysis) are motivated by concrete, well-documented failure modes of general-purpose agents (OpenHands), and the paper provides convincing efficiency evidence (2.2x more effective iterations, higher improvement rate).

Extensive ablations (data scaling, backbone sensitivity, model scale down to 3B) and detailed case studies/decision traces (e.g., PI4PC vs Mol Edit) provide genuine mechanistic insight rather than just aggregate numbers, and the paper is commendably candid about limitations (causal-reasoning gap, myopic data-filtering collapse).
Strong appendix supporting reproducibility: dataset statistics, baseline implementation protocols, full prompt architecture, and complete validation/test breakdowns.
weaknesses: Evaluation sets for many tasks are very small (e.g., AIME test=15, Mol Edit test=50, Visualization test=25), and no repeated runs/variance/seeds are reported despite the inherently stochastic nature of agentic rollouts, making several close margins (e.g., PI4PC tie at 44.00, Financial QA where Manual SFT/OpenHands are competitive) statistically difficult to trust.

FT-Agent does not uniformly dominate: it underperforms OpenHands on 3/13 tasks, sometimes substantially (Reaction Acc 38 vs 60, FTS 18.11 vs 35.59; Mol Und scaffold accuracy lower), and the main text does not clearly analyze why FT-Agent's specialized mechanisms fail on these cases beyond a brief note.

The Manual SFT baseline is constrained to an artificial 'two-pass' protocol that limits human iteration to match agent compute budget; this may understate real human-expert capability and makes the human-vs-agent comparison less representative of realistic expert practice.

The backend LLM (GPT-5.2/GPT-5) is used simultaneously as the agent's reasoning engine, as the data-synthesis/cleaning model, and as the LLM judge for evaluation, raising potential self-consistency/self-preference bias that is not discussed or controlled for.

The 'emergent capability' and 'causal reasoning gap' claims (Section 4.4, Appendix D) are drawn from single illustrative case studies (n=1 trajectories per phenomenon) rather than systematic quantitative analysis, so the generalizability of these qualitative conclusions is unclear.

Reproducibility is constrained by dependence on closed, rapidly-evolving proprietary models (GPT-5.2, GPT-5, GPT-4o-mini) for both the agent backbone and evaluation judge, which may make exact replication difficult as these APIs change or are deprecated.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely novel and well-motivated benchmark task: end-to-end autonomous LLM fine-tuning as an interactive agent problem, clearly distinguished from prior static-dataset MLE benchmarks (MLE-Bench, DSBench) by making both data construction and training configuration first-class optimization targets.

Comprehensive system design: standardized task interface, shared raw-data repository, sandboxed execution, structured multi-level feedback (metrics, per-instance predictions, loss curves), and a strict validation/test separation protocol that supports reproducibility.

FT-Agent's three mechanisms (structured iteration planning, fail-fast progressive validation, structured feedback analysis) are clearly motivated by concrete failure modes observed in general-purpose agents (OpenHands), and ablations (Table 3, Appendix C) quantitatively substantiate the efficiency gains (2.2x more effective iterations, higher improvement rate).

Reasonably thorough empirical validation: 13 tasks/5 domains, multiple baselines (manual SFT, tool-augmented OpenHands, frontier agents Codex/Claude Code, open-source planning backbones), ablations over data scale, backbone, and target model size, plus 3-run variance reporting for the main method.

Rich qualitative case studies and full decision traces (Appendix D, G) that transparently show both emergent capabilities (cross-domain data mixing, cumulative learning) and clear failure modes (myopic filtering causing data collapse, shotgun debugging without causal diagnosis), which strengthens the honesty and interpretability of the evaluation.

Explicit and appropriate framing of the benchmark's contribution as a protocol/infrastructure rather than new static datasets, and honest acknowledgment of the constrained nature of the Manual SFT baseline and limited model-scale coverage.
weaknesses: Several evaluation splits are extremely small (e.g., AIME 2025 has only 15 test examples out of 30 total filtered instances; several chemistry/patent subtasks have 100 or fewer test instances), making point estimates and even the reported 3-run std highly uncertain; the headline AIME 'breakthrough' (11.11% vs 0%) is based on very few examples and could be sensitive to a handful of lucky/unlucky samples.

Comparison rigor is asymmetric: FT-Agent is run 3 times with reported variance, while OpenHands, Manual SFT, and most frontier-agent baselines are run only once (justified by compute budget), which weakens the strength of head-to-head claims, especially for close scores.

The Manual SFT baseline is explicitly stated as not an expert upper bound and is artificially constrained (two-pass protocol, no LLM assistance in the main comparison), which may unfairly favor FT-Agent in the main table; the more fairly matched LLM-assisted Manual SFT variant (Table 6) only covers 5 of 13 tasks and shows FT-Agent's edge shrinking or reversing (e.g., AIME, Mol Edit comparable or Manual SFT ahead on some).

The frontier-agent and open-source backbone comparisons (Table 4) are limited to only 5 of the 13 tasks, leaving the majority of the benchmark without stronger controlled baselines beyond OpenHands, limiting confidence in the generality of 'FT-Agent achieves the best performance on 10/13 tasks' claim relative to stronger competitors.

On several metrics FT-Agent is clearly worse than OpenHands (e.g., Reaction Prediction FTS 30.92 vs 35.59, Reaction Acc 35.33 vs 60.00), indicating the framework's advantage is not uniform and is concentrated in specific task types (data-sparse, structurally constrained, code-generation tasks); this nuance could be more prominently discussed rather than framed mainly around the 10/13 headline.
The AIME evaluation relies partly on an LLM-as-judge (GPT-5) for correctness, which introduces potential judge bias/variance that is not independently validated against human grading.

Decontamination and leakage-prevention procedures between the raw training repository and evaluation benchmarks are asserted ('rigorous decontamination process') but not described in sufficient technical detail (e.g., method used, overlap thresholds) to allow independent verification.

Generalization claims are based on a single base model family/size pair (Qwen2.5-7B/3B); broader claims about the method's robustness across model scales and architectures remain speculative, as acknowledged by the authors themselves.

strengths: Novel and timely task formulation: treating end-to-end LLM fine-tuning (data construction + training configuration + iterative refinement via multi-level feedback) as an interactive agent task is a meaningful step beyond fixed-dataset MLE benchmarks like MLE-Bench/DSBench.

The benchmark suite is reasonably comprehensive (13 tasks, 5 domains) and well documented in the appendix, including dataset provenance, decontamination procedure, evaluation splits, and metric definitions, which aids reproducibility.

FT-Agent's three mechanisms (structured iteration planning, fail-fast validation, structured multi-level feedback analysis) are clearly motivated by concrete failure modes observed in general-purpose agents (OpenHands), and each is tied to a specific challenge.

The paper makes a genuine effort at controlled comparison: identical tools, sandbox, backbone LLM, and wall-clock budget across FT-Agent and OpenHands; it also adds frontier-agent baselines (Codex, Claude Code), open-source backbone variants, and a budget-sensitivity check, which strengthens the isolation of the proposed framework's contribution.

The case studies (Mol_Edit cumulative learning vs. PI4PC shotgun debugging, Visualization data collapse) provide genuinely useful qualitative insight into current agent limitations (causal reasoning, long-horizon/myopic planning), which is valuable for the community even beyond the headline numbers.
weaknesses: Very small held-out evaluation sets undermine the reliability of headline claims: many test splits are capped at 100 examples, and the flagship AIME 2025 result relies on only 15 test instances, meaning each correct/incorrect answer shifts accuracy by ~6.7 percentage points; the reported 11.11%±3.82% 'breakthrough' is not statistically well-supported at this scale.

The central claim of 'best performance on 10 of 13 tasks' is based on comparing FT-Agent's 3-run mean against single-run baselines with no significance testing; several wins are marginal (e.g., Data Analysis 34.71 vs. 32.78 baseline) and could plausibly fall within noise given the large standard deviations observed elsewhere (e.g., Reaction FTS 30.92±11.22).

The Manual SFT baseline is explicitly resource- and tool-constrained (no LLM assistance, two-pass protocol only) while FT-Agent freely leverages GPT-5/GPT-4o-mini for data synthesis and GPT-5.2 for orchestration; although the paper adds a partial LLM-assisted Manual SFT check on 5/13 tasks, this asymmetry weakens the main 13-task comparison's interpretability as evidence of agentic superiority over human practice.

Backbone/model generality claims are only partially substantiated: the ablation on planning backbones and on 3B vs. 7B target models is restricted to 5 of the 13 tasks, so claims of the framework 'transferring across planners' and target scales are not verified across the full benchmark.

Heavy reliance on proprietary GPT-5.2/GPT-5 (for orchestration, data synthesis, and as LLM judge) raises reproducibility concerns for the community (cost, access, and potential drift of closed models over time) and a subtle circularity risk in tasks like AIME, where GPT-5 both helps synthesize training data and serves as the correctness judge for the same pipeline's outputs.

The compute cost of full evaluation (single NVIDIA B200 GPU per run, 12-hour budgets, >1500 GPU-hours for full multi-seed baseline coverage) is very high, limiting practical reproducibility for most academic labs; only FT-Agent gets multi-run statistics while all comparison baselines are single runs, which is acknowledged but still weakens the robustness of cross-method comparisons.

The novelty of FT-Agent's mechanisms (structured planning, fail-fast validation, feedback aggregation) is more an engineering/orchestration contribution than an algorithmic advance, and the paper's own case studies show the agent still exhibits shallow, pattern-matching 'shotgun debugging' behavior (PI4PC) and catastrophic planning failures (Visualization data collapse), suggesting the proposed mechanisms only partially address the stated challenges.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated task formalization: casts end-to-end LLM fine-tuning (joint optimization of data construction and training configuration under iterative feedback) as an interactive agent task, clearly differentiated from prior MLE agent benchmarks (MLE-Bench, DSBench) that assume fixed datasets.

Comprehensive benchmark construction: 13 tasks across 5 domains with a shared raw-data repository, sandboxed execution, standardized Meta API/Evaluator interfaces, explicit decontamination procedures, and a principled validation/test split protocol (Nval=Ntest=min(100, n/2)).

FT-Agent's three-stage design (structured iteration planning, fail-fast progressive validation, structured multi-level feedback analysis) is directly motivated by concretely identified failure modes of general-purpose agents (OpenHands), and each mechanism is empirically supported (e.g., iteration counts, improvement rates in Table 3/8).

Strong effort at controlled comparison: baselines are equipped with identical tools (LlamaFactory/OpenCompass wrappers), same base model, same GPU/budget, and same backbone LLM where applicable, isolating the effect of agent orchestration design from tool availability.

Extensive experimental scope: main results, frontier-agent comparisons (Codex, Claude Code), open-source backbone ablations, data-scaling ablations, target-model-scale ablations, budget-sensitivity checks, and multi-run variance reporting for the main method.

Good transparency and honest limitations discussion: explicitly frames Manual SFT as not an expert upper bound, reports an LLM-assisted Manual SFT variant to scope comparisons fairly, and openly discusses causal-reasoning and long-horizon planning limitations via detailed case studies (e.g., PI4PC "shotgun debugging" trace).
High reproducibility support: detailed appendices document prompts (four-phase pipeline), dataset statistics, evaluator rubrics, baseline implementation details, and full validation/test results.
weaknesses: Statistical rigor is uneven: FT-Agent is run 3 times while competing baselines (OpenHands, Manual SFT, frontier agents) are single runs, which weakens the strength of head-to-head comparisons, especially on high-variance tasks (e.g., Reaction FTS 30.92±11.22).

Absolute performance remains low on several tasks (e.g., AIME ~11-13%, Reaction ~35%, many Table QA/Chemistry metrics well under 60%), raising questions about whether autonomous fine-tuning at this stage is a practically useful substitute for expert-driven pipelines rather than a research probe.

FT-Agent underperforms baselines on 3/13 tasks (e.g., Reaction Prediction, some Table QA metrics) without deep analysis of why the framework's mechanisms fail there, leaving an incomplete picture of its boundary conditions.

Potential data leakage/contamination concerns are not fully addressed: raw data and evaluation benchmarks are public, and synthetic CoT/data augmentation is performed by strong LLMs (GPT-5/GPT-4o-mini) that may have prior exposure to these benchmarks, which could inflate results in ways not disentangled from genuine agentic capability.

The controlled frontier-agent and backbone-generality comparisons (Table 4) are restricted to only 5 of the 13 tasks, limiting how strongly the paper's broader claims about agent design superiority can be generalized across the full task suite.

Cost/practicality trade-offs (FT-Agent relies on an expensive GPT-5.2 backbone and consumes more iterative budget than OpenHands) are reported but not deeply analyzed in terms of real-world deployment feasibility.

The benchmark's contribution is explicitly not new datasets but rather standardized interfaces around existing public datasets; while this is honestly disclosed, it modestly reduces the degree of methodological/data novelty relative to fully new benchmark construction.
